nameStory: The woodland crocus gets its name from its preference for naturalized settings under trees and shrubs, where it forms cheerful colonies that peek through the forest floor. It's also called Tommasini's crocus after Muzio G. Spirito de Tommasini, a 19th-century botanist who studied plants in southeastern Europe. Gardeners often affectionately call them 'tommies' for short!
description: Woodland crocus is a small, early-blooming bulb that stands just 3-4 inches tall when flowering. It produces delicate, cup-shaped flowers that emerge directly from the ground, often pushing through snow or leaf litter. The narrow, grass-like leaves have distinctive white stripes running down their centers and appear alongside or just after the flowers. This cheerful little plant spreads naturally over time, creating colorful carpets in late winter and early spring.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Six-petaled, goblet-shaped flowers in shades of purple, lavender, or white, often with darker purple veining on the outside that creates beautiful striped patterns when closed

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves with prominent white stripes down the center, feeling smooth and slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Flowers emerge directly from the ground on short stems, often appearing before the leaves are fully developed, creating clusters of blooms at soil level

idTips.label: Timing
idTips.description: Among the earliest crocuses to bloom, often flowering in late February or March while snow may still be present

habitat: Woodland crocus thrives in partially shaded areas under deciduous trees and shrubs, where it can receive spring sunlight before leaves emerge. It prefers well-drained soil and is commonly found naturalized in woodland gardens, parks, and older residential areas throughout New England. Look for established colonies near historic homes and in areas where bulbs have been planted and allowed to spread naturally.

seasonality.spring: The main show happens now, with flowers appearing from late February through March, followed by narrow striped leaves that photosynthesize to feed next year's bloom.
seasonality.summer: Leaves die back completely by early summer, leaving no trace above ground as the bulb rests underground.
seasonality.fall: Completely dormant with no visible growth, though the bulb is preparing for next spring's spectacular emergence.
seasonality.winter: Flower buds may begin pushing through soil or mulch during warm spells in late winter, often surprising gardeners with their early appearance.

funFact: Woodland crocuses are like nature's meteorologists – their flowers open and close based on temperature and light, staying tightly shut on cloudy, cold days and opening wide when the sun warms them, creating a daily flower show that changes with the weather!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other early crocus species, but woodland crocus typically has more slender flowers and is among the very first to bloom. The white-striped leaves are a good identifying feature, and unlike some crocuses, these often have beautiful purple striping on the outside of the petals that's visible when flowers are closed.
contextualKnowledge: Many people call this 'snow crocus' or 'early crocus,' but these names are shared with several other species, leading to confusion at garden centers. The horticultural nickname 'tommies' helps distinguish them from other early-blooming crocuses and refers specifically to this species.
compareHints: Woodland crocus blooms earlier than the larger spring crocus (Crocus vernus) and has more delicate, slender flowers. Unlike the bright yellow snow crocus (Crocus chrysanthus), woodland crocus comes in purple and white shades with distinctive outer striping. Its flowers are also typically smaller and more numerous than most other crocus species commonly grown in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Spring crocus is larger than its cousin the snow crocus, which blooms slightly earlier and has smaller, more delicate flowers.
Spring crocus blooms slightly later than snow crocus and has more elongated, pointed petals compared to the broader, rounder petals of Dutch crocus.
Snow crocus is the smallest and earliest blooming of the common crocuses in New England.
Among New England crocuses, silvery crocus is distinguished by its particularly pale coloring and the dark striping on outer petals.
**Comparison details uncertain due to limited data.
Unlike the common spring crocuses found throughout New England, Bieberstein's crocus blooms in fall rather than spring.
Among New England crocuses, Sieber's crocus is distinguished by its orange gradient effect on the petals, which fades from the brilliant orange stamens down through the bottom third of each petal.
Unlike the common Spring Crocus which blooms in March-April with white, purple, or yellow flowers, Kotschy's Crocus blooms in fall with pale lilac-blue flowers.
